claim: 105 malaria-endemic countries were identified based on 2000 P. falciparum and P. vivax prevalence estimates.
source: We identified 105 malaria-endemic countries based on 2000 P. falciparum and P. vivax prevalence estimates (before the scale-up of interventions), of which 44, 9, and 52 were endemic for P. falciparum only, P. vivax only, and co-endemic for both species, respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of prevalence data from the year 2000

claim: 44 countries were endemic for P. falciparum only in 2000.
source: We identified 105 malaria-endemic countries based on 2000 P. falciparum and P. vivax prevalence estimates (before the scale-up of interventions), of which 44, 9, and 52 were endemic for P. falciparum only, P. vivax only, and co-endemic for both species, respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of prevalence data from the year 2000

claim: 9 countries were endemic for P. vivax only in 2000.
source: We identified 105 malaria-endemic countries based on 2000 P. falciparum and P. vivax prevalence estimates (before the scale-up of interventions), of which 44, 9, and 52 were endemic for P. falciparum only, P. vivax only, and co-endemic for both species, respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of prevalence data from the year 2000

claim: 52 countries were co-endemic for both P. falciparum and P. vivax in 2000.
source: We identified 105 malaria-endemic countries based on 2000 P. falciparum and P. vivax prevalence estimates (before the scale-up of interventions), of which 44, 9, and 52 were endemic for P. falciparum only, P. vivax only, and co-endemic for both species, respectively.
evidence: Based on analysis of prevalence data from the year 2000

claim: The global clinical burden of malaria was focused in settings of high transmission intensity endemic for P. falciparum only.
source: Globally, the clinical burden of malaria was focused in settings of high transmission intensity endemic for P. falciparum only, followed by low-transmission settings co-endemic for P. falciparum and P. vivax (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1A

claim: 89% of the global population at risk of malaria was located in co-endemic settings with very low and low transmission intensities.
source: Conversely, 89% of the global population at risk of malaria was located in co-endemic settings with very low and low transmission intensities (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: All 25 countries with high transmission intensity were in Africa.
source: All 25 countries with high transmission intensity and 11 of 17 countries with moderate transmission intensity were in Africa, while almost half of global cases and populations at risk in low-transmission co-endemic settings originated in India.
evidence: Based on analysis of country-level transmission data

claim: 11 of 17 countries with moderate transmission intensity were in Africa.
source: All 25 countries with high transmission intensity and 11 of 17 countries with moderate transmission intensity were in Africa, while almost half of global cases and populations at risk in low-transmission co-endemic settings originated in India.
evidence: Based on analysis of country-level transmission data

claim: Almost half of global cases and populations at risk in low-transmission co-endemic settings originated in India.
source: All 25 countries with high transmission intensity and 11 of 17 countries with moderate transmission intensity were in Africa, while almost half of global cases and populations at risk in low-transmission co-endemic settings originated in India.
evidence: Based on analysis of country-level transmission data

claim: The relationship between ITN usage and malaria infection outcomes varied by the baseline entomological inoculation rate (EIR).
source: In model simulations, the relationship between ITN usage and malaria infection outcomes varied by the baseline entomological inoculation rate (EIR), representing local transmission intensity, and parasite species (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on model simulations shown in Figure 2

claim: The relationship between ITN usage and malaria infection outcomes varied by parasite species.
source: In model simulations, the relationship between ITN usage and malaria infection outcomes varied by the baseline entomological inoculation rate (EIR), representing local transmission intensity, and parasite species (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on model simulations shown in Figure 2

claim: The same increase in ITN usage achieved a larger relative reduction in clinical incidence in low-EIR than in high-EIR settings.
source: The same increase in ITN usage achieved a larger relative reduction in clinical incidence in low-EIR than in high-EIR settings.
evidence: Based on model simulations

claim: Low levels of ITN usage were sufficient to eliminate malaria in low-transmission settings.
source: Low levels of ITN usage were sufficient to eliminate malaria in low-transmission settings, whereas high ITN usage was necessary to achieve a substantial decrease in clinical incidence in high-EIR settings.
evidence: Based on model simulations

claim: High ITN usage was necessary to achieve a substantial decrease in clinical incidence in high-EIR settings.
source: Low levels of ITN usage were sufficient to eliminate malaria in low-transmission settings, whereas high ITN usage was necessary to achieve a substantial decrease in clinical incidence in high-EIR settings.
evidence: Based on model simulations

claim: At the same EIR value, ITNs led to a larger relative reduction in P. falciparum than P. vivax clinical incidence.
source: At the same EIR value, ITNs also led to a larger relative reduction in P. falciparum than P. vivax clinical incidence.
evidence: Based on model simulations

claim: ITN usage of 80% was not sufficient to lead to the full elimination of either P. falciparum or P. vivax in the highest transmission settings.
source: However, ITN usage of 80% was not sufficient to lead to the full elimination of either P. falciparum or P. vivax in the highest transmission settings.
evidence: Based on model simulations

claim: ITNs could reduce global P. falciparum cases by 83.6% from 252.0 million, assuming a maximum ITN usage of 80%.
source: In combination, the models projected that ITNs could reduce global P. falciparum and P. vivax cases by 83.6% from 252.0 million and by 99.9% from 69.3 million in 2000, respectively, assuming a maximum ITN usage of 80%.
evidence: Based on model projections

claim: ITNs could reduce global P. vivax cases by 99.9% from 69.3 million, assuming a maximum ITN usage of 80%.
source: In combination, the models projected that ITNs could reduce global P. falciparum and P. vivax cases by 83.6% from 252.0 million and by 99.9% from 69.3 million in 2000, respectively, assuming a maximum ITN usage of 80%.
evidence: Based on model projections

claim: The optimal strategies for reducing total malaria cases and for case reduction and pre-elimination were similar to the strategy that prioritized funding for high-transmission settings.
source: We found that the optimal strategies for reducing total malaria cases (i.e. global burden) and for case reduction and pre-elimination to be similar to the strategy that prioritized funding for high-transmission settings.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy for case reduction, case reduction and pre-elimination, and prioritizing high-transmission settings achieved reductions of 76%, 73%, and 66% at the intermediate budget level, respectively.
source: These three strategies achieved the largest reductions in global malaria cases at all budgets, including reductions of 76%, 73%, and 66% at the intermediate budget level, respectively (Figure 3A, Table 1).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 3A and Table 1

claim: At low to intermediate budgets, the proportional allocation strategy reduced malaria cases effectively by up to 53%.
source: At low to intermediate budgets, the proportional allocation strategy also reduced malaria cases effectively by up to 53%.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy for case reduction averted up to 31% more cases than prioritization of high-transmission settings.
source: Depending on the available budget, the optimal strategy for case reduction averted up to 31% more cases than prioritization of high-transmission settings and 64% more cases than proportional allocation, corresponding to respective differences of 37.9 and 74.5 million cases globally.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy for case reduction averted up to 64% more cases than proportional allocation.
source: Depending on the available budget, the optimal strategy for case reduction averted up to 31% more cases than prioritization of high-transmission settings and 64% more cases than proportional allocation, corresponding to respective differences of 37.9 and 74.5 million cases globally.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: There is a trade-off between reducing global cases and reducing the global population at risk of malaria.
source: We additionally found there to be a trade-off between reducing global cases and reducing the global population at risk of malaria.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Both the optimal strategies and the strategy prioritizing high-transmission settings did not achieve substantial reductions in the global population at risk until large investments were reached.
source: Both the optimal strategies and the strategy prioritizing high-transmission settings did not achieve substantial reductions in the global population at risk until large investments were reached (Figure 3B, Table 1).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 3B and Table 1

claim: At a high budget, the global population at risk was only reduced by 19% under the scenario prioritizing high-transmission settings.
source: Even at a high budget, the global population at risk was only reduced by 19% under the scenario prioritizing high-transmission settings, with higher reductions of 42–58% for the optimal strategies, while proportional allocation had almost no effect on this outcome.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: At a high budget, the optimal strategies achieved reductions of 42-58% in the global population at risk.
source: Even at a high budget, the global population at risk was only reduced by 19% under the scenario prioritizing high-transmission settings, with higher reductions of 42–58% for the optimal strategies, while proportional allocation had almost no effect on this outcome.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Proportional allocation had almost no effect on reducing the global population at risk.
source: Even at a high budget, the global population at risk was only reduced by 19% under the scenario prioritizing high-transmission settings, with higher reductions of 42–58% for the optimal strategies, while proportional allocation had almost no effect on this outcome.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing low-transmission settings achieved a 56% reduction in the global population at risk at intermediate budgets.
source: Conversely, diverting funding to prioritize low-transmission settings was highly effective at increasing the number of settings eliminating malaria, achieving a 56% reduction in the global population at risk already at intermediate budgets.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing low-transmission settings led to only a minimal reduction of 24% in total malaria case load at intermediate budgets.
source: However, this investment only led to a minimal reduction of 24% in total malaria case load (Figure 3, Table 1).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 3 and Table 1

claim: At high budget levels, prioritizing low-transmission settings resulted in up to 3.8 times (a total of 159.4 million) more cases than the optimal allocation for case reduction.
source: At high budget levels, prioritizing low-transmission settings resulted in up to 3.8 times (a total of 159.4 million) more cases than the optimal allocation for case reduction.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy for case reduction and pre-elimination led to pre-elimination in more malaria-endemic settings than all other strategies.
source: Despite the population at risk remaining relatively large with the optimal strategy for case reduction and pre-elimination, it nevertheless led to pre-elimination in more malaria-endemic settings than all other strategies (Appendix 1—figure 7), in addition to close to minimum cases across all budgets (Figure 3).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Appendix 1—figure 7 and Figure 3

claim: Case reductions generally occurred first for P. falciparum except when prioritizing low-transmission settings.
source: The allocation strategies also had differential impacts on P. falciparum and P. vivax cases, with case reductions generally occurring first for P. falciparum except when prioritizing low-transmission settings.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: P. vivax cases were not substantially affected at low global budgets for all allocation strategies except when prioritizing low-transmission settings.
source: P. vivax cases were not substantially affected at low global budgets for all other allocation strategies, and proportional allocation had almost no effect on reducing P. vivax clinical burden at any budget (Figure 3C), leading to a temporary increase in the proportion of total cases attributable to P. vivax relative to P. falciparum.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 3C

claim: Proportional allocation had almost no effect on reducing P. vivax clinical burden at any budget.
source: P. vivax cases were not substantially affected at low global budgets for all other allocation strategies, and proportional allocation had almost no effect on reducing P. vivax clinical burden at any budget (Figure 3C), leading to a temporary increase in the proportion of total cases attributable to P. vivax relative to P. falciparum.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 3C

claim: With very low to low budget levels, as much as 85% of funding was allocated to moderate to high transmission settings under the optimized strategy for case reduction.
source: With very low to low budget levels, as much as 85% of funding was allocated to moderate to high transmission settings (Figure 4A, Appendix 1—figure 8A).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 4A and Appendix 1—figure 8A

claim: The maximum ITN usage of 80% was reached in settings of high transmission intensity and smaller population sizes even at low budgets under the optimized strategy.
source: This allocation pattern led to the maximum ITN usage of 80% being reached in settings of high transmission intensity and smaller population sizes even at low budgets, while maintaining lower levels in low-transmission settings with larger populations (Figure 4B, Appendix 1—figure 8B).
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 4B and Appendix 1—figure 8B

claim: The proportion of the budget allocated to low and very low transmission settings increased with increasing budgets under the optimized strategy.
source: The proportion of the budget allocated to low and very low transmission settings increased with increasing budgets, and low transmission settings received the majority of funding at intermediate to maximum budgets.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Low transmission settings received the majority of funding at intermediate to maximum budgets under the optimized strategy.
source: The proportion of the budget allocated to low and very low transmission settings increased with increasing budgets, and low transmission settings received the majority of funding at intermediate to maximum budgets.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Settings endemic for only P. falciparum were prioritized at low to intermediate budgets under the optimized strategy.
source: Similar patterns were also observed for the optimized distribution of funding between settings endemic for only P. falciparum compared to P. falciparum and P. vivax co-endemic settings (Figure 4C–D), with the former being prioritized at low to intermediate budgets.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results shown in Figure 4C-D

claim: At the maximum budget, 70% of global funding was targeted at low- and very low-transmission settings co-endemic for both parasite species under the optimized strategy.
source: At the maximum budget, 70% of global funding was targeted at low- and very low-transmission settings co-endemic for both parasite species.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Results remained similar when assuming a linear relationship between ITN usage and distribution costs.
source: Results remained similar when assuming a linear relationship between ITN usage and distribution costs (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: Based on sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 10

claim: At high budgets, dynamic re-allocation of funding every 3 years led to the same case reductions over time as a one-time optimization with constant ITN usage.
source: At high budgets, capturing dynamic changes over time through re-allocation of funding based on minimizing P. falciparum cases every 3 years led to the same case reductions over time as a one-time optimization with the allocation of a constant ITN usage (Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: Based on dynamic re-allocation analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11

claim: At lower budgets, re-allocation every 3 years achieved a higher impact at several timepoints, but total cases remained similar between the two approaches.
source: At lower budgets, re-allocation every 3 years achieved a higher impact at several timepoints, but total cases remained similar between the two approaches.
evidence: Based on dynamic re-allocation analysis

claim: Reallocation of resources from settings which achieved elimination to higher transmission settings reduced total spending over the 39 year period in some cases.
source: Although reallocation of resources from settings which achieved elimination to higher transmission settings did not lead to substantially fewer cases, it reduced total spending over the 39 year period in some cases (Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: Based on dynamic re-allocation analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 11

claim: Optimizing ITN allocation to minimize global clinical incidence could avert 83% of clinical cases compared to no intervention at a high budget.
source: We estimated that optimizing ITN allocation to minimize global clinical incidence could, at a high budget, avert 83% of clinical cases compared to no intervention.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy to minimize clinical incidence and maximize pre-elimination averted 82% of clinical cases at a high budget.
source: In comparison, the optimal strategy to minimize the clinical incidence and maximize the number of settings reaching pre-elimination averted 82% of clinical cases, prioritizing high-transmission settings 81%, proportional allocation 61%, and prioritizing low-transmission settings 37%.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing high-transmission settings averted 81% of clinical cases at a high budget.
source: In comparison, the optimal strategy to minimize the clinical incidence and maximize the number of settings reaching pre-elimination averted 82% of clinical cases, prioritizing high-transmission settings 81%, proportional allocation 61%, and prioritizing low-transmission settings 37%.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Proportional allocation averted 61% of clinical cases at a high budget.
source: In comparison, the optimal strategy to minimize the clinical incidence and maximize the number of settings reaching pre-elimination averted 82% of clinical cases, prioritizing high-transmission settings 81%, proportional allocation 61%, and prioritizing low-transmission settings 37%.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing low-transmission settings averted 37% of clinical cases at a high budget.
source: In comparison, the optimal strategy to minimize the clinical incidence and maximize the number of settings reaching pre-elimination averted 82% of clinical cases, prioritizing high-transmission settings 81%, proportional allocation 61%, and prioritizing low-transmission settings 37%.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing low-transmission settings achieved elimination in 42% of settings when 50% of the maximum budget had been spent.
source: Prioritizing low-transmission settings achieved elimination in 42% of settings and reduced the global population at risk by 56% when 50% of the maximum budget had been spent, but also resulted in 3.2 times more clinical cases than the optimal allocation scenario.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Prioritizing low-transmission settings resulted in 3.2 times more clinical cases than the optimal allocation scenario when 50% of the maximum budget had been spent.
source: Prioritizing low-transmission settings achieved elimination in 42% of settings and reduced the global population at risk by 56% when 50% of the maximum budget had been spent, but also resulted in 3.2 times more clinical cases than the optimal allocation scenario.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The 20 highest-burden countries would need to obtain 88% of global investments to reach case and mortality risk estimates in alignment with GTS goals.
source: Previous research supports this approach, finding that the 20 highest-burden countries would need to obtain 88% of global investments to reach case and mortality risk estimates in alignment with GTS goals (Patouillard et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patouillard et al., 2017

claim: The modeled optimized funding strategy allocated up to 76% of very low budgets to settings of high transmission intensity located in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: This is similar to the modeled optimized funding strategy presented here, which allocated up to 76% of very low budgets to settings of high transmission intensity located in sub-Saharan Africa.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: Targeting interventions to local hot-spots has been shown to lead to higher cost savings than universal application.
source: Even within a single country, targeting interventions to local hot-spots has been shown to lead to higher cost savings than universal application (Barrenho et al., 2017), and could lead to elimination in settings where untargeted interventions would have little impact (Bousema et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barrenho et al., 2017

claim: Targeting interventions to local hot-spots could lead to elimination in settings where untargeted interventions would have little impact.
source: Even within a single country, targeting interventions to local hot-spots has been shown to lead to higher cost savings than universal application (Barrenho et al., 2017), and could lead to elimination in settings where untargeted interventions would have little impact (Bousema et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bousema et al., 2012

claim: Most of global funding should only be focused in low-transmission settings co-endemic for P. falciparum and P. vivax at high budgets once ITN use has already been maximized in high-transmission settings.
source: Our results suggest that most of global funding should only be focused in low-transmission settings co-endemic for P. falciparum and P. vivax at high budgets once ITN use has already been maximized in high-transmission settings.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: With a focus on disease burden reduction, a temporary increase in the proportion of malaria cases attributable to P. vivax was projected.
source: For example, with a focus on disease burden reduction, a temporary increase in the proportion of malaria cases attributable to P. vivax was projected, in line with recent observations in near-elimination areas (Battle et al., 2019; Price et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on model projections and supported by citations to Battle et al., 2019 and Price et al., 2020

claim: When international funding for malaria increased between 2007-2009, African countries remained the major recipients of financial support, while P. vivax-dominant countries were not as well funded.
source: Nevertheless, even when international funding for malaria increased between 2007–2009, African countries remained the major recipients of financial support, while P. vivax-dominant countries were not as well funded (Snow et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Snow et al., 2010

claim: Over 100 countries have eliminated malaria from near global endemicity in the 1900s.
source: From near global endemicity in the 1900's over 100 countries have eliminated malaria, with 10 of these certified malaria-free by the World Health Organization (WHO) in the last two decades (Feachem et al., 2010; Shretta et al., 2017; Weiss et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feachem et al., 2010; Shretta et al., 2017; Weiss et al., 2019

claim: 10 countries were certified malaria-free by the WHO in the last two decades.
source: From near global endemicity in the 1900's over 100 countries have eliminated malaria, with 10 of these certified malaria-free by the World Health Organization (WHO) in the last two decades (Feachem et al., 2010; Shretta et al., 2017; Weiss et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Feachem et al., 2010; Shretta et al., 2017; Weiss et al., 2019

claim: 41% of the global population in 2017 were estimated to live in areas at risk of infection with Plasmodium falciparum.
source: Despite this success, 41% and 57% of the global population in 2017 were estimated to live in areas at risk of infection with Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, respectively (Weiss et al., 2019; Battle et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weiss et al., 2019

claim: 57% of the global population in 2017 were estimated to live in areas at risk of infection with Plasmodium vivax.
source: Despite this success, 41% and 57% of the global population in 2017 were estimated to live in areas at risk of infection with Plasmodium falciparum and Plasmodium vivax, respectively (Weiss et al., 2019; Battle et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Battle et al., 2019

claim: In 2021 there were an estimated 247 million new malaria cases.
source: In 2021 there were an estimated 247 million new malaria cases and over 600,000 deaths, primarily in children under 5 years of age (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b

claim: In 2021 there were over 600,000 malaria deaths, primarily in children under 5 years of age.
source: In 2021 there were an estimated 247 million new malaria cases and over 600,000 deaths, primarily in children under 5 years of age (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b

claim: Global eradication of malaria could save millions of lives and offer high returns on investment.
source: Nevertheless, the global community continues to strive towards the ultimate aim of eradication, which could save millions of lives and thus offer high returns on investment (Chen et al., 2018; Strategic Advisory Group on Malaria Eradication, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2018 and Strategic Advisory Group on Malaria Eradication, 2020

claim: The GTS 2016-2030 goals include reducing malaria incidence and mortality rates by 90%.
source: The global goals outlined in the Global Technical Strategy for Malaria (GTS) 2016–2030 include reducing malaria incidence and mortality rates by 90%, achieving elimination in 35 countries, and preventing re-establishment of transmission in all countries currently classified as malaria-free by 2030 (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015

claim: The GTS 2016-2030 goals include achieving elimination in 35 countries by 2030.
source: The global goals outlined in the Global Technical Strategy for Malaria (GTS) 2016–2030 include reducing malaria incidence and mortality rates by 90%, achieving elimination in 35 countries, and preventing re-establishment of transmission in all countries currently classified as malaria-free by 2030 (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015

claim: The GTS 2016-2030 goals include preventing re-establishment of transmission in all countries currently classified as malaria-free by 2030.
source: The global goals outlined in the Global Technical Strategy for Malaria (GTS) 2016–2030 include reducing malaria incidence and mortality rates by 90%, achieving elimination in 35 countries, and preventing re-establishment of transmission in all countries currently classified as malaria-free by 2030 (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2015

claim: Various stakeholders have set timelines for global eradication ranging from 2030-2050.
source: Various stakeholders have also set timelines for the wider goal of global eradication, ranging from 2030–2050 (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2020, Chen et al., 2018; Strategic Advisory Group on Malaria Eradication, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to World Health Organization, 2020; Chen et al., 2018; Strategic Advisory Group on Malaria Eradication, 2020

claim: The global population at risk of malaria reduced from around 70% of the world population in 1950 to 50% in 2000.
source: Historically, large progress was made in eliminating malaria mainly in lower-transmission countries in temperate regions during the Global Malaria Eradication Program in the 1950s, with the global population at risk of malaria reducing from around 70% of the world population in 1950 to 50% in 2000 (Hay et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hay et al., 2004

claim: Renewed commitment to malaria control in the early 2000s with the Roll Back Malaria initiative extended the focus to the highly endemic areas in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Renewed commitment to malaria control in the early 2000s with the Roll Back Malaria initiative subsequently extended the focus to the highly endemic areas in sub-Saharan Africa (Feachem et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Feachem et al., 2010

claim: The current tool set is insufficient in itself to eradicate the malaria parasite.
source: Whilst it is now widely acknowledged that the current tool set is insufficient in itself to eradicate the parasite, there continues to be debate about how resources should be allocated (Snow, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Snow, 2015

claim: International donors represent 68% of the global investment in malaria control and elimination activities.
source: Global strategies are influenced by international donors, which represent 68% of the global investment in malaria control and elimination activities (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b

claim: The global investment for malaria control and elimination falls short of the 6.8 billion USD currently estimated to be needed to meet GTS 2016-2030 goals.
source: Given that the global investment for malaria control and elimination still falls short of the 6.8 billion USD currently estimated to be needed to meet GTS 2016–2030 goals (World Health Organization, 2007; World Health Organization, 2022b), an optimized strategy to allocate limited resources is critical to maximizing the chance of successfully achieving the GTS goals and longer-term eradication aspirations.
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2022b

claim: ITNs provide both an individual protective effect and population-level transmission reductions.
source: Whilst in reality, national malaria elimination programs encompass a broad range of preventative and therapeutic tools alongside different surveillance strategies as transmission decreases, this simplification is made for computational feasibility, with ITNs chosen as they (a) provide both an individual protective effect and population-level transmission reductions (i.e. indirect effects); (b) are the most widely used single malaria intervention other than first-line treatment; and (c) extensive distribution and costing data are available that allow us to incorporate their decreasing technical efficiency at high coverage.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about ITN mechanisms

claim: ITNs are the most widely used single malaria intervention other than first-line treatment.
source: Whilst in reality, national malaria elimination programs encompass a broad range of preventative and therapeutic tools alongside different surveillance strategies as transmission decreases, this simplification is made for computational feasibility, with ITNs chosen as they (a) provide both an individual protective effect and population-level transmission reductions (i.e. indirect effects); (b) are the most widely used single malaria intervention other than first-line treatment; and (c) extensive distribution and costing data are available that allow us to incorporate their decreasing technical efficiency at high coverage.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about malaria interventions

claim: The P. falciparum model has been fitted to age-stratified data from a variety of sub-Saharan African settings.
source: The P. falciparum model has previously been fitted to age-stratified data from a variety of sub-Saharan African settings to recreate observed patterns in parasite prevalence (PfPR2-10), the incidence of clinical disease, immunity profiles, and vector components relating to rainfall, mosquito density, and the EIR (Griffin et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Griffin et al., 2016

claim: The P. vivax model was originally calibrated to data from Papua New Guinea.
source: We developed a deterministic version of an existing individual-based model of P. vivax transmission, originally calibrated to data from Papua New Guinea but also shown to reproduce global patterns of P. vivax prevalence and clinical incidence (White et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2018

claim: The P. vivax model has been shown to reproduce global patterns of P. vivax prevalence and clinical incidence.
source: We developed a deterministic version of an existing individual-based model of P. vivax transmission, originally calibrated to data from Papua New Guinea but also shown to reproduce global patterns of P. vivax prevalence and clinical incidence (White et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2018

claim: As population coverage of ITNs increases, the marginal cost of distribution increases.
source: Previous studies have shown that, as population coverage of ITNs increases, the marginal cost of distribution increases as well (Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bertozzi-Villa et al., 2021

claim: The unit cost of distributing an ITN was assumed to be $3.50.
source: The cost associated with a given simulated ITN usage was calculated by multiplying the number of nets distributed per capita per year by the population size and by the unit cost of distributing an ITN, assumed to be $3.50 (Sherrard-Smith et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrard-Smith et al., 2022

claim: National governments of endemic countries contribute 31% of all malaria-directed funding globally.
source: National governments of endemic countries contribute 31% of all malaria-directed funding globally (World Health Organization, 2020), and government financing is a major source of malaria spending in near-elimination countries in particular (Haakenstad et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to World Health Organization, 2020

claim: Government financing is a major source of malaria spending in near-elimination countries.
source: National governments of endemic countries contribute 31% of all malaria-directed funding globally (World Health Organization, 2020), and government financing is a major source of malaria spending in near-elimination countries in particular (Haakenstad et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haakenstad et al., 2019

claim: Subnational malaria elimination in localized settings within a country can provide motivation for continued elimination in other areas.
source: Subnational malaria elimination in localized settings within a country can also provide motivation for continued elimination in other areas and friendly competition between regions to boost global elimination efforts (Lindblade and Kachur, 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lindblade and Kachur, 2020

claim: At high budgets, 62% of funding was targeted to low-transmission settings co-endemic for P. falciparum and P. vivax under the optimal strategy.
source: However, at high budgets, 62% of funding was targeted to low-transmission settings co-endemic for P. falciparum and P. vivax.
evidence: Based on optimization analysis results

claim: The optimal strategy for case reduction mirrored an allocation framework that prioritizes funding for high-transmission settings.
source: The optimal strategy for case reduction mirrored an allocation framework that prioritizes funding for high-transmission settings, resulting in total case reductions of 76% and 66% at intermediate budget levels, respectively.
